subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's Lemonade Stand and Priya's Shop
hook: Arun sells lemonade. Priya buys. Can they count money correctly?

slides.title: Money: Counting Rupees and Making Change
slides.inSimpleWords: Learn how to count money, make purchases, and understand profit.

slides.title: Summer Lemonade Business
slides.storyContext: It is summer in Delhi. Arun sets up a lemonade stand with Priya's help. A glass costs 5 rupees. On day one, Arun sells 8 glasses. How much money does he earn? Priya pulls out her notebook to calculate.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Street corner. Hot day. Colorful lemonade stand. Line of customers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun and Priya run a lemonade stand together.

image.alt: Summer Lemonade Business — Money

slides.title: Indian Money: Rupees and Paise
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'In India, we use rupees (Rs). 100 paise = 1 rupee. Coins: 1 Rs, 2 Rs, 5 Rs, 10 Rs. Notes: 10 Rs, 20 Rs, 50 Rs, 100 Rs.' Arun nods, counting his coins.

points.label: Value
points.text: 100 paise = 1 rupee

points.label: Coins
points.text: 1 Rs, 2 Rs, 5 Rs, 10 Rs are common

points.label: Notes
points.text: 10 Rs, 20 Rs, 50 Rs, 100 Rs are used daily

slides.inSimpleWords: One rupee equals one hundred paise always.

image.alt: Indian Money: Rupees and Paise — Money

slides.title: First Customers Arrive
slides.storyContext: By 10 AM, three customers have already bought lemonade. Each pays with coins. Arun places them in a small box. Priya watches carefully. 'We should count after each customer to make sure we are not losing track,' she suggests.

points.label: Action
points.text: Customer 1 pays 5 Rs. Customer 2 pays 10 Rs. Customer 3 pays 5 Rs.

slides.inSimpleWords: The first customers are happy with cold, refreshing lemonade.

slides.title: Arun's Daily Earnings
slides.storyContext: Arun sold 8 glasses at 5 Rs each. 'That is 8 times 5,' says Priya. They count: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 40 Rs. Arun earns 40 rupees in one day.

example.problem: 8 glasses at 5 Rs each. Total earnings?

slides.inSimpleWords: Eight glasses times five rupees equals forty total.

image.alt: Arun's Daily Earnings — Money

slides.title: Coins and Notes: Which to Use?
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arun: 'We can make 10 rupees with two 5-rupee coins OR one 10-rupee note. Some customers give notes, some give coins. We need to know both ways!'

points.label: Coins make
points.text: 5+5 = 10 Rs (two fives)

points.label: Simpler
points.text: One 10-rupee note = same value

slides.inSimpleWords: Many coins can equal one note of higher value.

slides.title: Priya's Change Problem
slides.storyContext: A customer gives a 20-rupee note for one glass (5 Rs). 'What do I give back?' asks Arun, confused. Priya says, 'You owe change. 20 - 5 = 15 rupees back. Give three 5-rupee coins!'

points.label: Concept
points.text: Change = amount paid - price of item

slides.inSimpleWords: Change is the money left after you pay for something.

slides.title: Making Change Correctly
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches Arun: 'To give change, always subtract the price from what they paid. Check: the price plus the change should equal what they paid.'

points.label: Formula
points.text: Change = Price paid - Item cost

points.label: Check
points.text: Change + Item cost = Price paid

points.label: Example
points.text: Paid 20 Rs, item = 5 Rs, change = 15 Rs. Check: 15 + 5 = 20. Correct!

slides.inSimpleWords: Always subtract to find change, then add to check.

slides.title: More Customers, More Change
slides.storyContext: A customer buys 2 glasses at 5 Rs each (10 Rs total) and pays with a 20-rupee note. Priya calculates: 'That is 10 Rs, so change is 20 - 10 = 10 Rs. One 10-rupee note back, or two 5-rupee coins.'

example.problem: Buy 2 glasses at 5 Rs each, pay 20 Rs. Change?
example.solution: Cost = 10 Rs. Change = 20 - 10 = 10 rupees. Give one 10 Rs note or two 5 Rs coins.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two glasses cost ten rupees, so change is ten.

slides.title: Adding Money
slides.storyContext: Arun earns 40 Rs on day one, 50 Rs on day two, and 35 Rs on day three. 'How much altogether?' asks Priya. She adds: 40 + 50 + 35 = 125 Rs.

points.label: Add
points.text: 40 Rs + 50 Rs + 35 Rs = 125 Rs

points.label: Method
points.text: Line up the rupees and add

slides.inSimpleWords: Add rupees together like regular numbers.

image.alt: Adding Money — Money

slides.title: Tracking Daily Sales
slides.storyContext: By the end of three days, Priya has written down each day's earnings on a notepad. She shows Arun: Day 1: 40 Rs, Day 2: 50 Rs, Day 3: 35 Rs. 'If we add them, we know our total success,' she says.

points.label: Tracking helps
points.text: Know exactly how much money you have

slides.inSimpleWords: Write down money earned each day to stay organized.

slides.title: Buying Supplies
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya visit the market. Lemons cost 20 Rs per kilogram. Sugar: 15 Rs. Bottles: 30 Rs. Total cost for supplies: 20 + 15 + 30 = 65 Rs. 'We spend 65 Rs,' says Priya.

example.problem: Lemons (20 Rs) + sugar (15 Rs) + bottles (30 Rs) = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty plus fifteen plus thirty equals sixty-five.

image.alt: Buying Supplies — Money

slides.title: Costs: Money Spent
slides.storyContext: Priya explains to Arun: 'Cost is the money we pay to buy things we need for the business. We have to spend money to make money!'

points.label: Cost
points.text: Money spent to buy supplies and materials

points.label: Tracking
points.text: Always write down what you spend

points.label: Reason
points.text: To know if you truly made a profit

slides.inSimpleWords: Costs are the expenses of running a business.

slides.title: Profit and Money Left
slides.storyContext: Arun earned 40 Rs on day one. He spent 65 Rs on supplies. 'Do we have enough?' asks Priya. 'After day two we will!' says Arun. 40 + 50 = 90 Rs, minus 65 Rs cost = 25 Rs profit.

points.label: Profit
points.text: Money earned minus money spent = profit

slides.inSimpleWords: Profit equals earnings minus the cost of supplies.

image.alt: Profit and Money Left — Money

slides.title: The Big Money Moment
slides.storyContext: By day three, Arun and Priya count all their money: 125 Rs earned total. They spent 65 Rs on supplies. 'We have 125 - 65 = 60 Rs profit!' Priya celebrates. 'We made a real profit, Arun!'

points.label: Achievement
points.text: They turned a business idea into real profit

slides.inSimpleWords: They earned one hundred twenty-five and spent sixty-five.

slides.title: Calculating Profit from Days 1-3
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a simple table: Days 1-3 earnings = 40 + 50 + 35 = 125 Rs. Total costs = 65 Rs. Profit = 125 - 65 = 60 Rs. Arun smiles: 'We really did it!'

example.problem: Total earned 125 Rs. Spent 65 Rs on supplies. Profit?
example.solution: Profit = 125 - 65 = 60 rupees. Both earn 30 Rs each if they split it!

slides.inSimpleWords: One hundred twenty-five minus sixty-five equals sixty.

slides.title: Arun Wants a Prize
slides.storyContext: Arun sees a toy for 100 Rs. He earned 125 Rs total. If he spends 100 Rs on the toy, how much money does he have left?
slides.inSimpleWords: One hundred twenty-five minus one hundred equals twenty-five.

image.alt: Arun Wants a Prize — Money

slides.title: Can They Buy More Supplies?
slides.storyContext: With 60 Rs profit, can Arun and Priya buy new supplies (65 Rs) for week two? Or do they need to earn more first? What should they do?

points.label: Think
points.text: Profit 60 Rs < New costs 65 Rs. They need 5 more Rs!

slides.inSimpleWords: They do not have enough profit to buy all new supplies.

slides.title: Money Saving Strategy
slides.storyContext: Priya proposes: 'Let's keep our profit and just buy a little more stock this week. We will earn more money and save to buy supplies in bigger amounts.' Arun agrees. Teamwork and planning make the business grow!

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Smart money management = thinking ahead

slides.inSimpleWords: Saving money helps businesses grow bigger over time.

slides.title: Rupees to Paise Conversion
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: 'Sometimes you need smaller money. 1 rupee = 100 paise. So 5 rupees = 500 paise. If you give someone 1 rupee and 50 paise for a 2-rupee item, is that enough?' Arun nods: 'No! That is only 150 paise, less than 200.'

points.label: Convert
points.text: 1 rupee = 100 paise

points.label: Example
points.text: 5 rupees = 500 paise

points.label: Mix
points.text: 2 rupees 50 paise = 250 paise total

slides.inSimpleWords: Rupees and paise can be converted back and forth.

slides.title: Comparing Coin Values
slides.storyContext: Arun asks: 'I have ten 1-rupee coins. Do I have as much as someone with two 5-rupee coins?' Priya calculates: 'Ten ones = 10 rupees. Two fives = 10 rupees. Exactly the same!'

example.problem: Compare: 10 one-rupee coins vs. 2 five-rupee coins
example.solution: Both equal 10 rupees. Coins don't matter, value does.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different coins can have the same total value.

slides.title: A Big Unexpected Order
slides.storyContext: On day four, a neighborhood party asks Arun and Priya: 'Can you make 20 glasses by 5 PM?' That is 20 × 5 = 100 Rs earning potential. But supplies now cost 80 Rs! Profit would be 100 - 80 = 20 Rs. 'Should we take the big order?' asks Arun.

points.label: Opportunity
points.text: More sales = more profit IF costs stay manageable

slides.inSimpleWords: Bigger orders mean bigger profits but bigger risks.

slides.title: Budgeting for Business Growth
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'We have 60 Rs profit saved. The big order costs 80 Rs, so we are 20 Rs short. We can skip the order, or we can use some saved profit to take the order and earn more.' Arun learns smart financial planning.

points.label: Budget
points.text: Plan what you have and what you need to spend

points.label: Strategy
points.text: Use profits wisely to grow bigger

points.label: Risk
points.text: Sometimes investing profit leads to bigger profits

slides.inSimpleWords: Good planning helps businesses grow smart and safe.

slides.title: Week Two: The Big Order Success
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya decide to invest their 60 Rs profit. They spend 80 Rs total (60 profit + 20 Rs extra from parents' loan) and earn 100 Rs. Profit this time: 100 - 80 = 20 Rs. Plus they repay parents 20 Rs. Still earn 0 Rs net, BUT now they have customers for week three!

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Sometimes you lose money now to earn more later

slides.inSimpleWords: Business growth needs patience and smart decisions.

slides.title: Winter Stock vs. Summer Prices
slides.storyContext: Priya notices: 'In summer, we charge 5 Rs a glass because it is hot and everyone buys. In winter, fewer people buy. Should we drop to 3 Rs to sell more?' Arun thinks: 'At 3 Rs we need to sell 16 to earn 48. At 5 Rs we only need 10 sales. Which is smarter?'

points.label: Think
points.text: Price high, sell fewer. Price low, sell more. What makes more money?

slides.inSimpleWords: Pricing strategy affects both volume and profit.

slides.title: Loss and Break-Even Point
slides.storyContext: A day, Arun spends 65 Rs on supplies but only sells 10 glasses for 50 Rs total. 'We lost 15 Rs today!' says Priya. Arun nods: 'We need to sell at least 13 glasses to break even (13 × 5 = 65). Anything over 13 is profit.'

example.problem: Supplies cost 65 Rs. Each glass is 5 Rs. How many glasses to break even?
example.solution: Break-even = 65 ÷ 5 = 13 glasses. Sell 13 or more to make profit or break even.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break-even is when earnings equal costs with zero profit.

slides.title: Arun and Priya's Success
slides.storyContext: By end of summer, Arun bought the toy and still has 25 Rs left. 'We learned addition, subtraction, and money together,' says Priya. 'And multiplication too!' adds Arun.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Money has units: rupees and paise

points.label: Remember
points.text: Add and subtract money like regular numbers

points.label: Remember
points.text: Profit = earnings minus costs

points.label: Remember
points.text: Plan, track, and grow your money wisely

slides.inSimpleWords: Using math with money helps you earn and save.

image.alt: Arun and Priya's Success — Money

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's School Day with Priya's Clock
hook: What time does school start? How long until lunch? Arun learns to read the clock.

slides.title: Time and Calendar: Hours, Minutes, Days, and Months
slides.inSimpleWords: Learn to read clocks, understand days and months, plan your schedule.

slides.title: Learning to Read the Clock
slides.storyContext: Arun's school day starts at 9:00 AM. He keeps asking Priya, 'Is it time for lunch yet?' By the fifth time, Priya says, 'Arun, I will teach you to read the clock so you can check yourself!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Classroom. Big wall clock. Priya pointing at the numbers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun wants to know when lunch time arrives each day.

image.alt: Learning to Read the Clock — Time and Calendar

slides.title: The Analog Clock Face
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'A clock has 12 numbers. The short hand shows the hour (like 9 for 9 o'clock). The long hand shows the minutes. It takes 60 minutes to make one full circle.'

points.label: Short hand
points.text: Hour hand—shows which hour (1 to 12)

points.label: Long hand
points.text: Minute hand—shows which minute (0 to 60)

points.label: 60 minutes
points.text: = 1 hour exactly

slides.inSimpleWords: A clock has two hands showing hours and minutes.

image.alt: The Analog Clock Face — Time and Calendar

slides.title: The Minute Hand Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arun looks confused. 'The long hand is longer, but it shows the minute? The short hand is shorter, but it shows the hour?' Priya nods: 'Yes! It is confusing at first, but you will get it. The name tells you what it does, not its size.'

points.label: Remember
points.text: Short hand = hour (moves slowly). Long hand = minute (moves faster).

slides.inSimpleWords: The names of the hands tell what they do.

slides.title: 9 o'Clock: School Starts
slides.storyContext: Priya points: 'When the short hand points to 9 and the long hand points to 12, it is 9:00 o'clock. School starts.'

example.problem: What time does the clock show: short hand at 9, long hand at 12?

slides.inSimpleWords: When both hands point up, it is exactly nine.

image.alt: 9 o'Clock: School Starts — Time and Calendar

slides.title: Minutes: Counting by Fives
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: 'Look at the minute hand numbers. They count by 5s: at 1 = 5 minutes, at 2 = 10 minutes, at 3 = 15 minutes, at 6 = 30 minutes.' Arun practices counting the big hand positions.

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Every number = 5 more minutes (1=5, 2=10, 3=15, etc.)

points.label: Key times
points.text: 6 = 30 minutes (half hour), 12 = 0 minutes (on the hour)

slides.inSimpleWords: Minutes jump by fives as the long hand moves.

slides.title: Minutes Past the Hour
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: 'When the long hand moves to 3, it means 15 minutes past. To 6 means 30 minutes past. To 9 means 45 minutes past.'

points.label: At 3
points.text: 15 minutes past the hour

points.label: At 6
points.text: 30 minutes past (half past)

points.label: At 9
points.text: 45 minutes past (quarter to next hour)

slides.inSimpleWords: Different positions of the minute hand show minutes.

image.alt: Minutes Past the Hour — Time and Calendar

slides.title: Quarter Hour Landmarks
slides.storyContext: Priya draws four quarter circles on a paper clock. 'Top = :00 (o'clock), right = :15 (quarter past), bottom = :30 (half past), left = :45 (quarter to). These are the main times most people remember!'

points.label: Key moments
points.text: Quarter hours are easier to spot than any minute

slides.inSimpleWords: Watch for quarter-past, half-past, and quarter-to times.

slides.title: 10:30 AM: Snack Time
slides.storyContext: The bell rings. Priya checks the clock: short hand between 10 and 11, long hand at 6. 'It is 10:30! Half past 10. Snack time, Arun!'

example.problem: Short hand between 10 and 11, long hand at 6. What time?

slides.inSimpleWords: The hand at six means thirty minutes past the hour.

image.alt: 10:30 AM: Snack Time — Time and Calendar

slides.title: 2:15 PM: Math Class
slides.storyContext: Arun looks at the clock during afternoon. Short hand points just past 2, long hand at 3. 'Is it 2:15?' he asks. Priya smiles. 'Yes! You are learning fast!'

example.problem: Short hand just past 2, long hand at 3. What time?

slides.inSimpleWords: The hand at three means fifteen minutes past.

slides.title: AM and PM: Morning and Afternoon
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'AM is before noon (morning). PM is after noon (afternoon and evening). 9 AM is morning start. 9 PM is night bedtime. The same numbers on the clock, but different times of day!'

points.label: AM
points.text: Midnight (12 AM) to just before noon (11:59 AM)

points.label: PM
points.text: Noon (12 PM) to just before midnight (11:59 PM)

points.label: Noon
points.text: Middle of the day = 12 PM

slides.inSimpleWords: AM means morning, PM means afternoon or night.

slides.title: Days and Months
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a calendar. 'Look, there are 7 days in a week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... And 12 months in a year: January, February...' Arun points to June: 'That is summer!'

points.label: Days
points.text: 7 days per week (Monday to Sunday)

points.label: Months
points.text: 12 months per year (January to December)

points.label: Dates
points.text: Days have numbers: 1 to 31

slides.inSimpleWords: Calendars show all days, weeks, and months.

image.alt: Days and Months — Time and Calendar

slides.title: School Schedule for the Week
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arun a weekly planner. 'Monday is Math, Tuesday is Science, Wednesday is Art, Thursday is PE, Friday is Hindi. You have classes each day!' Arun nods: 'And Saturday and Sunday are holidays!'

points.label: Pattern
points.text: School 5 days, rest 2 days

slides.inSimpleWords: Each day of the week has its own activities.

slides.title: Planning Month Activities
slides.storyContext: Arun's birthday is June 20. Summer vacation is June 20 to July 20. Priya marks both on the calendar. 'You have summer fun for one whole month!' Arun counts: about 30 days of freedom.

example.problem: Summer starts June 20 and ends July 20. How many days?
example.solution: About 30 days of summer holidays—almost one whole month!

slides.inSimpleWords: One month has about thirty days.

slides.title: What Time is Lunch?
slides.storyContext: Arun checks the clock himself. Short hand at 1, long hand at 12. 'Is it lunch time (1:00 PM)?' he asks Priya. She nods with a smile.

points.label: Try this
points.text: If school ends at 3:30 PM, where should the hands point?

slides.inSimpleWords: The short hand at one means one o'clock exactly.

image.alt: What Time is Lunch? — Time and Calendar

slides.title: How Many Days Until Diwali?
slides.storyContext: Priya points to October on the calendar. 'Diwali is October 15. Today is October 1. How many days until we celebrate?' Arun counts on the calendar: 14 days.

points.label: Count
points.text: October 1 to October 15 = 14 days of waiting

slides.inSimpleWords: Counting days on a calendar helps plan celebrations.

slides.title: Time for Every Activity
slides.storyContext: Arun now has a daily routine he tracks: 9:00 AM school start, 10:30 AM snack, 1:00 PM lunch, 2:15 PM math, 3:30 PM school end, 4:00 PM homework, 5:00 PM play. Every day has a schedule!

points.label: Benefit
points.text: Knowing time helps you manage the whole day

slides.inSimpleWords: A schedule keeps your day organized and on time.

slides.title: Seconds and Ticks
slides.storyContext: Priya adds: 'Actually, there is a THIRD hand on a clock—the second hand. It ticks once per second. 60 seconds = 1 minute. It moves the fastest.'

points.label: Second hand
points.text: The thin hand—moves every second

points.label: Pattern
points.text: 60 seconds = 1 minute (just like 60 minutes = 1 hour)

points.label: Speed
points.text: Fastest hand on the clock

slides.inSimpleWords: The second hand ticks once per second, sixty times per minute.

slides.title: Measuring Time for Activities
slides.storyContext: Priya times Arun doing homework: 'It took you 45 minutes. That is from 4:00 PM to 4:45 PM.' She shows on the clock: 'Long hand moved from 12 to 9. That is 45 minutes exactly.'

example.problem: If you start homework at 4:00 and finish at 4:45, how long did it take?
example.solution: 45 minutes. The minute hand moves from 12 to 9.

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure how long activities take using the minute hand.

slides.title: Daylight Saving and Seasons
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'In some countries, clocks change in spring and fall for daylight hours. In India, we do not do this. Our time stays the same all year. That is why India Standard Time (IST) is easy to remember!'

points.label: India
points.text: One time zone (IST) for the whole country

slides.inSimpleWords: India uses one time throughout the year.

slides.title: Digital vs. Analog Time
slides.storyContext: Arun sees a digital clock: 4:30. Priya asks: 'What time is that on an analog clock?' Arun points: 'Short hand between 4 and 5, long hand at 6.' Priya confirms: 'Both say the same thing!'

points.label: Analog
points.text: Clock with hands (traditional)

points.label: Digital
points.text: Clock with numbers (newer)

points.label: Same
points.text: Both show the exact same time

slides.inSimpleWords: Analog and digital clocks show time in different ways.

slides.title: How Long Until the Holiday?
slides.storyContext: Arun checks: 'Today is June 15. Summer holiday starts July 1. How many days?' Priya counts on a calendar: 'June 15 to June 30 = 15 days, plus 1 day in July = 16 days. More than 2 weeks!'

example.problem: June 15 to July 1. How many days?
example.solution: Count: 15 to 30 (15 days in June) + 1 (July 1) = 16 days total.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count days between dates on a calendar.

slides.title: Midnight and Noon Confusion
slides.storyContext: Arun asks: 'Is 12 o'clock noon or midnight?' Priya explains: '12:00 at daytime is noon (middle of the day, 12 PM). 12:00 at night is midnight (start of new day, 12 AM). Same number, different times!'

points.label: Noon
points.text: 12:00 PM in the middle of day (sun highest)

points.label: Midnight
points.text: 12:00 AM start of new day (darkest)

slides.inSimpleWords: Noon is midday, midnight is the start of night.

slides.title: Plan Your Whole Day by Clock
slides.storyContext: Arun tries: 'If I wake at 7:00 AM, eat at 7:30, go to school at 8:00, come home at 3:30, do homework until 5:00, then play until 6:30, when is my dinner?' Priya helps: 'Dinner is at 7:30 PM, which gives you 1 hour to play.'

points.label: Plan
points.text: Write down all times and calculate gaps between them

slides.inSimpleWords: Plan your day by writing down all the times.

slides.title: How Much Time Between Activities?
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'From 2:15 PM to 3:45 PM, how long is that?' Arun calculates: 'From 2:15 to 3:15 is 1 hour, then 3:15 to 3:45 is 30 more minutes. Total = 1 hour 30 minutes.'

example.problem: From 2:15 PM to 3:45 PM, how much time?

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate time between two clock readings.

slides.title: Arun Never Asks Again
slides.storyContext: From that day on, Arun reads the clock himself. 'Priya, remember when you taught me? Now I am the time keeper!' He checks his watch proud, ready for every activity.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Short hand = hour (1 to 12), long hand = minute (0 to 60)

points.label: Remember
points.text: 60 minutes = 1 hour, 7 days = 1 week, 12 months = 1 year

points.label: Remember
points.text: Read the short hand first, then the long hand

points.label: Remember
points.text: Plan your day using times to manage every activity

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading clocks helps you be on time always.

image.alt: Arun Never Asks Again — Time and Calendar

subject: Science
title: Arun's Garden and Priya's Plant Discovery
hook: Why do plants need roots? Priya digs deep to find out.

slides.title: Plants: Parts and Their Jobs
slides.inSimpleWords: Discover how roots, stems, leaves, and flowers work together to keep plants alive.

slides.title: Digging Up a Plant
slides.storyContext: Arun digs up a tomato plant from his garden. Priya sees roots, a thick stem, green leaves, and yellow flowers. 'Why does a plant have so many different parts?' she asks.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Arun's backyard garden in Pune. Soil, shovel, a tomato plant freshly pulled up.

slides.inSimpleWords: A plant has many parts, each with its own job.

image.alt: Digging Up a Plant — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: The Four Main Parts of a Plant
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a simple picture: 'Every plant has four parts: roots below ground, stem above ground, leaves on the stem, and flowers at the top. Each part does something important.'

points.label: Below ground
points.text: Roots—drink water

points.label: Main trunk
points.text: Stem—holds up everything

points.label: Green parts
points.text: Leaves—make food

points.label: Colorful parts
points.text: Flowers—make seeds

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants have roots, stems, leaves, and flowers.

slides.title: Roots: Drink Water and Hold On
slides.storyContext: Priya observes the roots—thin, thread-like strands underground. 'Roots drink water from the soil and hold the plant in the ground,' explains Arun. 'If I pull at the stem, the roots hold tight!'

points.label: Job 1
points.text: Absorb water and nutrients from soil

points.label: Job 2
points.text: Keep the plant anchored in the ground

points.label: Where
points.text: Roots grow underground

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots drink water and anchor plants firmly down.

image.alt: Roots: Drink Water and Hold On — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Why Plants Need Strong Roots
slides.storyContext: Arun shows Priya: 'See these old roots? Very thick and spread wide. That is why the tomato plant never blew over in the wind.' Priya nods: 'Roots are like the foundation of a house—they keep everything stable.'

points.label: Comparison
points.text: Roots = foundation, Stem = walls, Leaves/Flowers = roof

slides.inSimpleWords: Strong roots keep plants from falling in wind.

slides.title: Two Types of Roots
slides.storyContext: Priya asks, 'Why do some plants have thick roots like carrots, and others have thin thread-like roots?' Arun explains: 'This tomato has fibrous roots (many thin ones). A carrot has a taproot (one thick one that goes deep).'

example.problem: Why might a carrot store food in its root?
example.solution: The taproot stores nutrients to survive. That is why carrots are orange and crunchy!

slides.inSimpleWords: Different plants have different kinds of roots.

image.alt: Two Types of Roots — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Stem: Transport and Support
slides.storyContext: Priya feels the thick green stem of the tomato plant. 'The stem carries water from the roots to the leaves. It also holds up the leaves so they can catch sunlight,' says Arun.

points.label: Job 1
points.text: Transport water and nutrients to leaves and flowers

points.label: Job 2
points.text: Support the plant's weight

points.label: Example
points.text: A tree's trunk is its stem

slides.inSimpleWords: The stem carries water up and holds leaves high.

image.alt: Stem: Transport and Support — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Inside the Stem: Tiny Tubes
slides.storyContext: Priya imagines: 'Inside the stem, like water pipes in a house, are tiny tubes. They carry water up from the roots to every leaf and flower. That is why you must water plants—the water travels up through these tubes!'

points.label: Hidden system
points.text: Stems have internal tubes like plumbing

slides.inSimpleWords: Stems have tiny tubes that carry water everywhere.

slides.title: Leaves: Make Food for the Plant
slides.storyContext: Priya touches a green leaf. 'Why are leaves green?' she asks. Arun replies, 'Green is chlorophyll. It helps leaves catch sunlight and make food for the plant. Without leaves, the plant would starve!'

example.problem: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for a month. What happens?
example.solution: Without sunlight, leaves cannot make food. The plant dies or turns yellow/white.

slides.inSimpleWords: Green leaves make food using sunlight every day.

image.alt: Leaves: Make Food for the Plant — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Photosynthesis: How Leaves Work
slides.storyContext: Arun uses a simple idea: 'Leaves are like tiny kitchens. Sunlight is the heat, water from roots is the ingredient, and air goes in through holes in the leaf. The kitchen makes food (glucose) that the plant eats to grow!'

points.label: Simple formula
points.text: Sunlight + water + air = food + oxygen

points.label: Why green
points.text: Chlorophyll catches sunlight energy

points.label: Bonus
points.text: Plants release oxygen, which we breathe

slides.inSimpleWords: Leaves turn sunlight into food and oxygen.

slides.title: Flowers and Fruits: Make Seeds
slides.storyContext: Priya points to yellow flowers on the tomato plant. 'When flowers are pollinated by bees, they make fruits. Inside fruits are seeds,' explains Arun. 'Seeds grow into new plants!'

points.label: Flowers
points.text: Attract bees and butterflies for pollination

points.label: Fruits
points.text: Protect seeds inside

points.label: Seeds
points.text: Grow into new plants (reproduction)

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers become fruits, and fruits hold seeds inside.

image.alt: Flowers and Fruits: Make Seeds — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: From Flower to Tomato
slides.storyContext: Arun shows Priya small green tomatoes on the plant. 'Two weeks ago, these were flowers. Bees came, and the flowers turned into little green balls. Now they are growing bigger and will turn red. That is a tomato, and inside are many seeds!'

points.label: Process
points.text: Flower → green fruit → ripe fruit → seeds inside

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers transform into fruits as seeds develop.

slides.title: Plant Needs Detective
slides.storyContext: Priya takes a plant and: (1) Hides its roots in dark soil, (2) Puts it near a window, (3) Waters it daily. 'What does it need to grow?' she asks. Arun says, 'All three!'

points.label: Try this
points.text: What happens if a plant gets no water? No sunlight? No soil?

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need soil, water, sunlight, and air daily.

image.alt: Plant Needs Detective — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Comparing Plant Types
slides.storyContext: Priya brings different plants: a tall sunflower, a short grass, a succulent (no real leaves), and a cactus. 'Each looks different, but do they all have roots, stems, leaves, and flowers?' The answer is yes—just shaped differently!

points.label: Observation
points.text: All plants follow the same pattern, even if they look very different

slides.inSimpleWords: Every plant type has the same four basic parts.

slides.title: Plant Life Cycle: Seed to Plant
slides.storyContext: Priya shows the cycle: 'Seed → roots grow down, stem grows up → leaves appear → flowers bloom → fruits form → seeds fall out → new seeds grow into new plants. It is a circle of life!'

points.label: Stage 1
points.text: Seed germinates (sprouting)

points.label: Stage 2
points.text: Roots and stem develop

points.label: Stage 3
points.text: Leaves photosynthesize, flowers bloom

points.label: Stage 4
points.text: Fruits contain seeds, cycle repeats

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants go through a life cycle from seed to seed.

slides.title: How Pollination Happens
slides.storyContext: Priya watches a bee on the tomato flower. 'When the bee lands, pollen sticks to its body. The bee flies to another flower and drops pollen. This is pollination! Without bees, no fruits. Without fruits, no seeds.'

example.problem: A plant has many flowers but no bees visit. Will it make fruits?
example.solution: Unlikely. No bee pollination = no seeds = no fruits. Some plants can self-pollinate, but most need pollinators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bees help plants make fruits by spreading pollen.

slides.title: Arun Grows His Own Garden
slides.storyContext: By summer's end, Arun uses all he learned: he planted carrot seeds (long roots!), grew tomatoes (with Priya's care), watered daily (roots), checked for sunlight (leaves), watched flowers turn to fruit, and collected seeds to plant next year.

points.label: Journey
points.text: From curious questions to confident gardener in one season

slides.inSimpleWords: Learning about plants helps you grow your own garden.

slides.title: Edible Plant Parts We Eat
slides.storyContext: Priya laughs: 'We eat different parts of different plants! Carrots are roots, lettuce is leaves, broccoli is flowers, apples are fruits with seeds, and potatoes are underground stems!' Arun nods: 'Every plant part can be food for us!'

points.label: Roots to eat
points.text: Carrots, radishes, onions

points.label: Leaves to eat
points.text: Spinach, lettuce, cabbage

points.label: Flowers to eat
points.text: Broccoli, cauliflower

points.label: Fruits to eat
points.text: Tomatoes, apples, bananas

slides.inSimpleWords: Every part of a plant can be delicious and nutritious.

slides.title: What If a Plant Has No Leaves?
slides.storyContext: Arun brings a cactus to the garden. Priya studies it: 'This cactus has almost no leaves, just thick stems and spines! How does it make food?' Arun learns: 'The stem IS green! It makes food just like leaves do. Different plants, different designs.'

points.label: Adaptation
points.text: Desert plants modify leaves for water survival

slides.inSimpleWords: Some plants have adapted leaves in unusual shapes.

slides.title: Plant Needs: Water, Soil, Light, Air
slides.storyContext: Priya summarizes: 'For a plant to thrive: (1) Soil provides nutrients and anchor, (2) Water fills cells and transport, (3) Sunlight powers photosynthesis, (4) Air provides CO2 and oxygen exchange. All four are essential!'

points.label: Soil
points.text: Nutrients and support (from roots)

points.label: Water
points.text: Transport and cell filling (absorbed by roots)

points.label: Light
points.text: Energy for photosynthesis (caught by leaves)

points.label: Air
points.text: CO2 for food-making (stomata on leaves)

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need four things to survive: soil, water, light, and air.

slides.title: Why a Plant Wilts Without Water
slides.storyContext: Arun forgets to water a plant for 3 days. Leaves droop. Priya explains: 'Water keeps cells firm and full (turgid). Without water, cells collapse. Give it water, and in hours, the plant stands up again—the wilting is not permanent yet.'

example.problem: A plant wilts from no water for 3 days. Is it dead?
example.solution: Probably not. Water it immediately. If roots are alive, the plant will recover and stand firm again within hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wilting is reversible if you water quickly enough.

slides.title: Growing Beans in a Jar Experiment
slides.storyContext: Priya puts bean seeds in a wet jar against the glass with blotting paper. 'Let's watch roots grow DOWN and shoots grow UP.' Over 10 days, Arun sees: roots first (downward), then stem, then leaves (upward). 'Plants know which way is up and which way is down!'

points.label: Observation
points.text: Roots grow toward gravity (down). Shoots grow toward light (up).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants respond to gravity and light in their growth.

slides.title: Seasons and Plant Growth
slides.storyContext: Arun notices: 'In spring, plants grow quickly. In summer, they are full. In autumn, they slow down. In winter, many rest.' Priya nods: 'Different seasons suit different plants. That is why we plant tomatoes in spring, not winter!'

points.label: Seasonal timing
points.text: Spring and summer are growing seasons. Fall and winter are rest periods.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants have seasons for growth and rest.

slides.title: Flowering Times
slides.storyContext: Arun observes: 'Marigolds flower in autumn, jasmine at night, sunflowers in summer, tulips in spring.' Priya explains: 'Each plant has its own optimal flowering time based on temperature, daylight, and water availability. Nature is precise!'

example.problem: Why do different flowers bloom at different times of year?
example.solution: Plants evolved to flower when their pollinators (bees, butterflies) are active and when climate conditions are ideal for seed development.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different flowers bloom at different times of the year.

slides.title: Design Your Own Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya challenges Arun: 'If you plant carrots, tomatoes, and leafy greens together, what do you need to provide? Sunlight at which hour? Water how many times a week? Soil type?' Arun plans it all out using what he learned.

points.label: Plan
points.text: Consider each plant's needs and design the garden layout

slides.inSimpleWords: Use knowledge of plant parts to design a successful garden.

slides.title: Arun and Priya's Plant Wisdom
slides.storyContext: By season's end, both have learned: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, and fruits all work together. Each part has its job. A healthy plant is a team of parts!

points.label: Remember
points.text: Roots: absorb water, anchor plant

points.label: Remember
points.text: Stem: transport water, support leaves

points.label: Remember
points.text: Leaves: make food using sunlight

points.label: Remember
points.text: Flowers and fruits: make seeds for new plants

points.label: Remember
points.text: Every part of a plant serves a life purpose

slides.inSimpleWords: Each plant part does a special job for survival.
